title: Sharp feature-learning transitions and Bayes-optimal neural scaling laws in extensive-width networks
claim: Smaller students trained near an effective width outperform full-width ones and track optimal scaling laws, revealing a sharp width-data tradeoff.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, log-log plots with dashed theoretical slope lines
description: Three log-log line plots sit side by side. Left: test error against training epoch for a width-100 student (black), which dips and then rises, and a width-15 student (red), which keeps improving and ends lower. Faint curves show training error. Middle: generalization error against student width, with one curve per sample rate n/(kd) from 2 to 20, coloured from black through red to orange. Each curve is U-shaped, with a minimum at an intermediate width, and a dashed black line marks the predicted slope. Right: error against data size n for full width (black), effective width (blue), optimized width (red) and Bayes-optimal (purple). All curves fall as power laws with dashed slope guides. Shaded bands show standard deviation. The eye goes first to the left panel's diverging black and red curves, then to the U-shaped family in the middle.
caption: Adam-trained students (all curves except the purple one, right panel) on a teacher with $\sigma(x)=\tanh(2x)$ (with the $2x$ matching the convention in [ref]), $k=100$, $d=200$, $\Delta=0.01$, power-law readout with $\beta=1$ (3 batches, $10^4$ epochs, learning rate $0.003$; averages over 9 runs, shaded regions show $\pm 1$ standard deviation). Left: At fixed sample rate $n/(kd)=2$, a reduced-width student (solid = test error; faint = training error) outperforms the full-width one. Middle: Generalization error vs.\ student width $k_s$ at several sample rates $n/(kd)$. Performance degrades beyond a critical width; the dashed line indicates the theoretically predicted optimal model-size exponent $1-2\beta$. Right: Generalization error vs.\ data size $n$ for three width choices -- full-width ($k_s=k$), effective width ($k_s=k_c$ from theory), and optimized width (best-performing $k_s \in \{10,20,\ldots,100\}$ found by grid search) -- together with the Bayes-optimal prediction (purple). Dashed lines indicate the predicted scaling exponents: $1/(2 \beta) - 1$ in the feature-learning regime and $-1$ in the refinement regime, see Section [ref] and Appendix [ref] for the derivation of exponents.
abstract: We study the information-theoretic limits of learning a one-hidden-layer teacher network with hierarchical features from noisy queries, in the context of knowledge transfer to a smaller student model. We work in the high-dimensional regime where the teacher width $k$ scales linearly with the input dimension $d$ -- a setting that captures large-but-finite-width networks and has only recently become analytically tractable. Using a heuristic leave-one-out decoupling argument, validated numerically throughout, we derive asymptotically sharp characterizations of the Bayes-optimal generalization error and individual feature overlaps via a system of closed fixed-point equations. These equations reveal that feature learnability is governed by a sequence of sharp phase transitions: as data grows, teacher features become recoverable sequentially, each through a discontinuous jump in overlap. This sequential acquisition underlies a precise notion of \textit{effective width} $k_c$ -- the number of learnable features at a given data budget $n$ -- which unifies two distinct scaling regimes: a feature-learning regime in which the Bayes-optimal generalization error $\varepsilon^{\rm BO}$ scales as $ n^{1/(2Î²)-1}$, and a refinement regime in which it scales as $n^{-1}$, where $Î²>1/2$ is the exponent of the power-law feature hierarchy. Both laws collapse to the single relation $\varepsilon^{\rm BO}=Î(k_c d/n)$. We further show empirically that a student trained with \textsc{Adam} near the effective width $k_c$ achieves these optimal scaling laws (up to a small algorithmic gap), and provide an information-theoretic account of the associated scaling in model size.
